title: Trump's $100,000 H-1B Visa Fee Blocked Again As Second Federal Judge Halts Enforcement
text:

Swarajya Staff
Oct 02, 2026 | Updated 09:08 AM GMT+5:30

A federal judge in California has blocked United States President Donald Trump's $100,000 fee on new H-1B visas for highly skilled foreign workers, marking the second time a federal court has halted enforcement of the controversial policy.
US District Judge Haywood Gilliam in Oakland ruled on 30 September that US Citizenship and Immigration Services and the State Department failed to follow necessary rule-making processes before implementing the charge.
The ruling came in response to a lawsuit filed by a coalition of unions, employers and non-profit organisations, including healthcare, educational and religious groups.
Judge Gilliam granted a preliminary injunction preventing agencies from enforcing the fee until the Department of Homeland Security completes proper notice-and-comment rulemaking under the Administrative Procedure Act.
The decision applies to the September 2026 extension issued by the White House, which had attempted to maintain the fee through September 2027.
The controversial charge was first introduced in September 2025, dramatically increasing costs from the typical $1,500 to $3,800 range to $100,000 per petition.
Over 700 petitions included the payment before courts intervened, generating revenue but drawing widespread criticism from employers who argued the fee created insurmountable financial barriers.
The H-1B programme allows US companies to hire foreign workers in speciality occupations, with sectors including healthcare, education and technology heavily reliant on such visas.
In June, a federal judge in Massachusetts struck down the fee in a separate case brought by 20 states, concluding it functioned as an unauthorised tax requiring congressional approval.
The Trump administration appealed that ruling, but the US Court of Appeals for the First Circuit refused to pause the decision in July.
Meanwhile, the US Department of Homeland Security proposed a permanent fee of $103,265 through formal regulation in August, though that proposal would face fresh legal challenges once finalised.
The administration defended the policy by arguing the H-1B programme displaces American workers and undermines national security.
However, plaintiffs highlighted that visa holders play critical roles in addressing workforce shortages, particularly in healthcare services for an ageing population and teaching positions.
The US Justice Department has not announced whether it will appeal Judge Gilliam's ruling, though multiple legal challenges remain pending across federal courts nationwide.

Judge Gilliam granted a preliminary injunction preventing agencies from enforcing the fee until the Department of Homeland Security completes proper notice-and-comment rulemaking under the Administrative Procedure Act. Over 700 petitions included the payment before courts intervened, generating revenue but drawing widespread criticism from employers who argued the fee created insurmountable financial barriers.
